Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette: Amit, a 72-year-old man of South Eastern Asian descent, had spent the first half of his life tending children as a nanny while staying with his wife in a quiet suburban home. On a rain-slick evening in his late thirties, his romantic partner, whom he had married a year earlier, locked him in the dimly lit basement to "toughen him up." The darkness seemed to press against his chest as the partner's hand tightened around his throat, and the sound of shuffling feet filled the cramped space. In that instant, Amit felt the terror that had defined the entire episode, his body shuddering as if struck by an unseen blow. The memory of that night, he told the therapist, feels as though it belongs to someone else, a stranger's horror trapped in his mind. When the memory resurfaces, Amit is overcome with a wave of terror that feels identical to the original panic. The scene is vivid in his body: his limbs rigid, his breath shallow, his heart hammering. He has learned that thinking of the basement's flickering light will set off a startle response, and that a sudden movement-perhaps a creak of the stairs-will jolt him back into the same defensive posture. These reactions, he says, keep him on edge even in safe surroundings. Because the memory is so alien and frightening, he has come to believe that showing anger would only invite further violence, so he suppresses all anger, never allowing himself to feel or express it. By staying in a state of constant alertness and refusing to confront the past, he has begun to avoid any circumstance that reminds him of that dark night: he refuses to go into dim rooms, he resists any evening shifts that require him to be near a child's bedroom at night, and he shuns any event that might induce even mild stress. The fear of a sudden startle has seeped into his daily routine. In the workplace, he requests daytime hours and declines any assignments that involve late evenings or nighttime visits, even when a family needs an extra set of hands during school plays. The avoidance of darkness and stressors has made his job increasingly precarious, and the resulting decline in income has strained his relationship with his wife. The startle responses, the inability to relax, and the alien quality of the memory continually feed one another: a memory of terror sparks a threat reaction, which forces him into avoidance, which, in turn, reinforces the feeling that the memory is not his own but a replay of an external nightmare. Suppressing anger further blurs the memory, making it feel detached and alien, and the bodily reenactment he experiences whenever the memory flashes feels like a loop that refuses to break. Despite the clear pattern of avoidance, Amit remained silent for years, convinced that the past could not touch him anymore. Only after his wife pleaded with him to seek help-after he had missed an important bedtime for a child because the lights were too bright-did he agree to a counseling session. He fears that the cycle of startle and avoidance will destroy the small stability he has built in his later years, leaving him a shadow of his former self. He hopes, in the first tentative steps toward therapy, that learning to let his anger surface and facing the memory in a controlled way might loosen the tight grip of the dark basement's echo. The very thought of that possibility-of not being forced to stay on guard-gives him a glimmer of hope as he sits in the clinic, the therapist's calm voice a contrast to the sudden jostling of a memory still too close to his heart.
